checks.location: §4.1 Assumption 1 inheritance, text lines 162–166; invoked again in Appendix A
checks.claim: Singular-value interlacing supplies a positive parent lower bound for each generic row slice, including the default rank-r truncated source.
checks.explanation: A rank-truncated parent can have zero smallest singular value while every slice has full row rank. Interpreting the parent quantity as its smallest nonzero singular value does not repair the inequality: row selection can make a slice's positive singular values arbitrarily small.
checks.demonstration:
For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, take the rank-one source
$$W=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2}&0\\ \varepsilon&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Its singular values are $1$ and $0$. The two one-row slices have singular values $\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2}$ and $\varepsilon$, and each has condition number one. Thus the ordinary parent minimum is zero; if the minimum means the smallest nonzero value, the second slice violates $\varepsilon\ge1$. This is a valid top-one truncation of a full-rank pretrained matrix: add a singular component of size $1/2$ along the perpendicular left vector and second right coordinate. All positive $\varepsilon$ in this interval give the same failure.
checks.repair:
Keep slice regularity as an independent assumption. For $W=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^\top$ and an invertible $r\times r$ row block $U_{r,i}$, use
$$\sigma_{\min}(W_i)\ge\sigma_{\min}(U_{r,i})\,\sigma_r(W).$$
This follows from $W_i=U_{r,i}\Sigma_rV_r^\top$, orthonormality of $V_r$ and the minimum singular-value product bound. A uniform positive lower bound requires quantitative control of the row blocks, not just generic invertibility. The original interlacing argument does apply to a full-row-rank parent, because $W_iW_i^\top$ is a principal submatrix of the positive-definite matrix $WW^\top$.
checks.scope: This corrects the justification for inheriting Assumption 1 from a rank-truncated parent. It does not invalidate that assumption when it is explicitly imposed or refute the full-row-rank interlacing case.
checks.title: Row slicing does not inherit the claimed singular-value lower bound
checks.whyItMatters: Slice conditioning must be assumed or bounded using the selected rows, rather than inferred from the truncated parent alone.
checks.claimContext: Section 4.1 separately assumes full row rank and finite condition number for each slice. It then claims that generic row slicing and singular-value interlacing give $\sigma_{\min}(W_i)\ge\sigma_{\min}(W)>0$, including when $W$ is the default rank-$r$ truncation.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 4.1, setup, Assumption 1 and its interlacing justification; Section 3.3 default rank-r source.

checks.location: Proposition 1(ii), §4.2; Appendix B, text lines 1158–1183, extension to unconstrained delta
checks.claim: SVD left/right rotations coincide for every real shared scale vector delta, just as for the positive-spectrum rotation-only configuration.
checks.explanation: The algebraic factorization remains valid for signed scales, but an SVD must have nonnegative singular values. A negative scale can make the symmetric core indefinite, so it cannot be represented with one common rotation on both sides of a nonnegative SVD diagonal.
checks.demonstration:
Take $r=k=2$, $U=V=R=I_2$, $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$ and the allowed vector $\delta=(-2,0)$. Equation (3) gives
$$\widetilde W=\operatorname{diag}(-2,1).$$
If its in-basis SVD rotations were equal, then $\widetilde W=QDQ^\top$ for an orthogonal $Q$ and a diagonal $D\ge0$. Every such matrix is positive semidefinite, whereas the displayed matrix has eigenvalue $-2$. This contradicts part (ii), while leaving the signed-diagonal identity in part (i) intact.
checks.repair: Require $1+\delta_j\ge0$ for every $j$. Then $\Sigma\operatorname{diag}(1+\delta)$ is nonnegative and the source's common-rotation factorization is an SVD after a common permutation sorts its diagonal. The statement should assert the existence of compatible SVD bases, since repeated or zero singular values allow nonunique choices. Strictly positive scales avoid zero singular values. If arbitrary real scales are intended, state signed-diagonal coherence instead of SVD coherence; absorbing negative signs into just one singular basis generally makes the two rotations differ.
checks.scope: This concerns the unrestricted real-scale extension of Proposition 1(ii). Appendix B correctly handles the rotation-only case. The matrix example does not establish that a trained adapter ever takes a negative scale.
checks.title: Unrestricted spectrum scales do not preserve coherent SVD rotations
checks.whyItMatters: The proposition needs a positivity constraint, or a different meaning of coherence, when the spectrum is learned.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 1 allows every real scale vector $\delta\in\mathbb R^r$ and claims equal left and right SVD rotations. Appendix B proves the zero-scale case using a positive-semidefinite core, then says the same argument applies after replacing $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma\operatorname{diag}(1+\delta)$.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 4.2, Equation (3), Proposition 1(ii) and its unrestricted scale vector; Appendix B, extension of the positive-semidefinite argument.

checks.location: §5.2, text line 580, additive rank-r representability comparison; default W_lr construction in §§3.3 and 4.3
checks.claim: An additive rank-r update generally cannot realize the default CORA per-slice coherent adaptation.
checks.explanation: Independent slice rotations do not create new right directions in the default rank-$r$ construction. The resulting full weight change therefore has an exact additive rank-$r$ factorization. A parameterization may fail to enforce coherent rotations while still being able to represent them.
checks.demonstration:
Write the default source as $W_{\mathrm{lr}}=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^\top$ and set $P=V_rV_r^\top$. Each full-row-rank slice has row space $\operatorname{range}(V_r)$, so its thin right singular basis $V_i$ satisfies $V_iV_i^\top=P$. Equation (3) ends in $V_i^\top$, hence each adapted slice $\widetilde W_i$ obeys $\widetilde W_iP=\widetilde W_i$. After assembling the slices, both the adapted source and the original source lie in that same right subspace. Since the residual is frozen,
$$\Delta W=\widetilde W_{\mathrm{lr}}-W_{\mathrm{lr}},\qquad \Delta WP=\Delta W.$$
The factors $B=\Delta WV_r$ and $A=V_r^\top$ give $BA=\Delta W$ exactly. With the same frozen principal residual, the adapted source itself also admits rank-$r$ factors.
checks.repair: Describe the distinction as a constraint on the parameterization: CORA enforces coherent slice rotations directly, whereas unrestricted additive factors do not enforce them. Retain a representability comparison only after specifying additional restrictions that exclude the factorization above. A comparison involving a minor-component frozen residual, or the full-source CORA variant, requires its own analysis because those are different feasible sets.
checks.scope: This refutes the blanket additive-rank-r expressivity comparison for the default source. It does not establish equivalence to every constrained SVD-based adapter, and it does not challenge CORA's trainable parameter budget or optimization behavior.
checks.title: Default CORA updates fit within additive rank-r factors
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed distinction is enforced geometry, not an inability of unrestricted rank-r factors to express the default update.
checks.claimContext: Section 5.2 says that the additive low-rank update used by SVD-based adapters cannot in general realize CORA's coherent slice rotations. For the default construction, CORA adapts a rank-$r$ source and freezes its residual; under Assumption 1 every slice spans the same global right subspace.

checks.checkedLocation: Section 5.2, additive representability claim; Sections 3.3 and 4.2, default source and Equation (3); Assumption 1.

checks.location: Introduction, text line 47; repeated interpretation in §3.2 line 125; one-sided OFT defined in §2 line 90
checks.claim: One-sided orthogonal finetuning is a subset of the coherent two-sided in-basis rotation form, with zero spectrum shift.
checks.explanation: A one-sided rotation changes the left singular basis without making the corresponding right rotation. The coherent two-sided form requires a symmetric core in the original singular coordinates. These are different restrictions even for arbitrarily small, well-conditioned perturbations.
checks.demonstration:
Let $W_0=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, so $U_0=V_0=I_2$, and let
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0<|\theta|<\pi/2.$$
Then
$$RW_0=\begin{pmatrix}2\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\2\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$$
is not symmetric. Every coherent core $QDQ^\top$ is symmetric, even if signed diagonal entries are allowed, so it cannot equal $RW_0$. The update preserves singular values $2,1$ and condition number $2$. Moreover,
$$\frac{\|RW_0-W_0\|_F}{\|W_0\|_F}=2|\sin(\theta/2)|\longrightarrow0,$$
so a small-perturbation condition does not remove the example.
checks.repair: State that one-sided orthogonal finetuning preserves singular values, while coherent two-sided adaptation ties its two in-basis rotations. Neither fact makes the former a subset of the latter. The families with learned spectra are generally incomparable: the example above is one-sided but not coherent, whereas a coherent scaling such as $2W_0$ changes singular values and cannot be written as $RW_0$ with orthogonal $R$. A genuine zero-shift coherent subfamily is $U_0Q\Sigma_0Q^\top V_0^\top$; it should not be identified with ordinary one-sided orthogonal finetuning.
checks.scope: This corrects the claimed inclusion of parameterized matrix families. It does not criticize the singular-value preservation of orthogonal finetuning or the definition of CORA itself.
checks.title: One-sided orthogonal finetuning is not a coherent two-sided rotation
checks.whyItMatters: A spectrum-preserving update is not automatically an equal-rotation update.
checks.claimContext: The introduction defines orthogonal finetuning as $W=RW_0$ and then treats it as a special case of $U_0Q(\Sigma_0+\Delta\Sigma)Q^\top V_0^\top$ with zero spectrum shift. Preserving singular values does not impose equality of the left and right in-basis rotations.

The confident-error pixels change from positions \(\{1,4\}\) to \(\{1\}\), because position four falls back to its argmax without passing the confidence gate. Hence
\[(\mathrm{LER},\mathrm{DR}):\ (1/2,0)\longrightarrow(1/4,1/4).\]

\[G\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad\Delta G=\epsilon G.\]

\[Y=G^2-(G+\epsilon G)^2=-cG^2,\qquad a_1=\frac{-c\epsilon\mathbb E[G^3]}{\epsilon^2}=0.\]

checks.demonstration:
Choose the smooth activation \(\sigma(z)=z\), take \(p=d\), and collect independent standard Gaussian training vectors in \(X\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}\). Let \(W\), independent of \(X\), have independent standard Gaussian entries and put \(B=W/\sqrt d\), which is invertible almost surely. For a fixed \(t'>0\), write
\[a=e^{-2t'},\qquad C=aXX^\top/n+(1-a)I_d.\]
Then \(C\) is positive definite and the empirical feature moment is \(U=BCB^\top\). The exact score-regression normal equations give
\[s_\phi(x)=-B^\top(BCB^\top)^{-1}Bx=-C^{-1}x.\] In particular, the score is independent of \(W\), so conditioning on the input and its teacher-flow perturbation does not condition on the Gaussian feature matrix. The required conditional Gaussian feature property holds. The activation coefficients are exactly \(a_1^2=\mu_1^2=1\) and \(a_0=0\).

For the stated probability-flow step, direct expansion of the feature increment gives the coefficient of \(\Delta t^2\) as

Independence and concentration of \(B\) then make the limiting normalized trace of the proposed matrix at most
\[-\frac{a^2}{1-a^2}<0.\]
This cannot approximate the true positive semidefinite curvature. At \(t'=0.1\), the upper bound is approximately \(-2.0332\). All ratios stay in the required proportional regime, with \(p/d=1\) and \(n/d=1/2\). checks.contextBefore: We start with visual examples using Facebook DiT-XL (SD3 medium in Appendix). Figure 6(a)(i) compares the two extremes: an always-global denoiser produces a clean golden retriever, while an always-local denoiser gives “domains” of small dogs (with size comparable to $r$ ) smoothly merged together. This can be understood as the creative samples from Kamb and Ganguli (2024). Figure 6(a)(ii) shows that using the global denoiser during $[0.2,0.7]$ and a local conditioned denoiser outside that window preserves a globally coherent dog better than the reverse schedule. Figure 6(a)(iii) makes the separation from conditioning sharper: even when the outside-window local denoiser is unconditional, putting global denoising in the critical window remains helpful, whereas replacing the critical window by local denoising is much worse.
checks.contextAfter: Our work provides a unified operational view of two notions of phase transitions in diffusion models. By connecting symmetry breaking induced by conditioning with the onset of nonlocal computation in the score, we show that both phenomena can be detected through the same set of measurable quantities. This yields a concrete diagnostic for identifying when global communication is actually required during sampling, rather than assumed a priori from model design. In particular, the agreement (or mismatch) between instantaneous score-based probes and integrated sampling behavior directly reveals how efficiently a model uses its conditioning signal and attention mechanism over time.

checks.claim: The hybrid empirical baseline and normalization introduce no finite-sample bias; its baseline-score expectation vanishes.
checks.explanation: The zero-mean score identity cancels an action-independent baseline. It does not cancel the empirical hybrid mean, because rollout $j$ contributes its own reward and $\mathbb E[\bar R S_j]$ can be nonzero. The empirical standard deviation also depends on that rollout and cannot be dropped when expanding the normalized advantage. On-policy sampling alone does not justify either cancellation.
checks.demonstration:
Fix one input and let the policy ignore the images. Each mono-source and multi-source rollout independently draws $O\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, receives the permitted reward $R=1+O$, and has logit score $S=O-p$. Let $K=N+M$, and let $\bar R$ average all $K$ rewards. For an optimized rollout $j$, independence gives
$$\mathbb E[\bar R S_j]=\frac{p(1-p)}{K},\qquad
\mathbb E[(R_j-\bar R)S_j]=\left(1-\frac1K\right)p(1-p).$$
The baseline term discarded in Equation (22) is therefore nonzero.

Normalization does not recover the identity. Set $N=2$, $M=1$ and $p=1/3$. Enumerating the eight possible rollout groups gives expected hybrid gradient $2\sqrt2/9\approx0.31427$ with the population standard deviation. The standard two-rollout normalized estimator and the expected-reward gradient both equal $2/9\approx0.22222$. Groups with zero variance have zero advantage.

Using the sample standard deviation gives normalized expectations approximately $0.25660$ and $0.15713$, respectively, so that convention does not restore equality either. Adding the implementation's $10^{-6}$ denominator stabilizer leaves these rounded values unchanged.
checks.repair:
For at least two conditionally independent rollouts and rewards with no explicit parameter dependence, use the leave-one-out baseline
$$b_{-j}=\frac1{K-1}\sum_{\ell\ne j}R_\ell$$
and remove the random group standard deviation. Assume the policy has parameter-independent support and differentiation can pass through its probability integral, so $\mathbb E[S_j\mid x]=0$. Conditional on the complete input $x$, $b_{-j}$ is independent of rollout $j$, giving
$$\mathbb E[b_{-j}S_j\mid x]=0,\qquad\mathbb E[(R_j-b_{-j})S_j\mid x]=\mathbb E[R_jS_j\mid x].$$
Averaging over optimized rollouts and inputs gives the expected-reward gradient. A fixed global divisor $c>0$ gives the known rescaling $\nabla J/c$. This proves the alternative estimator's property but changes MARS normalization. Retaining the empirical group divisor requires an analysis of that estimator's bias, rather than the exact cancellation claimed in Theorem 3.1.
checks.scope: The counterexample refutes Theorem 3.1's finite-sample expectation identity and the baseline cancellation in Appendix A.2. A leave-one-out baseline without random scaling gives an unbiased expected-reward gradient under the stated independence and score-regularity conditions, but changes the published estimator. The separate decomposition and threshold corrections do not remove this bias.
checks.title: The empirical hybrid baseline biases the policy-gradient estimate
checks.claimContext: Theorem 3.1 claims that the hybrid normalized advantage in Equation (5) has the same expected policy gradient as on-policy optimization. The hybrid mean and standard deviation are estimated from the same $N$ multi-source and $M$ mono-source rollouts, while only the multi-source rollouts contribute score terms.
checks.whyItMatters: Theorem 3.1 justifies hybrid normalization by claiming that it preserves the on-policy gradient $\nabla_\theta J$. The shared empirical baseline and random scale invalidate the steps used to establish that identity.

checks.claim: The exact normalized hybrid gradient equals the standard normalized gradient plus the printed information-gain regularizer.
checks.explanation: The appendix's numerator decomposition is valid. Dividing by the hybrid standard deviation does not turn its first term into the standard multi-source normalized update unless the divisors agree. The information-gain term also needs the hybrid divisor. These batch-dependent scales cannot be removed as one fixed common constant.
checks.demonstration:
Write \(\alpha=N/(N+M)\) and \(\Delta_{IG}=\mu_{\rm multi}-\mu_{\rm mono}\). Let $S_j=\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(O_j)$, $\overline S=N^{-1}\sum_jS_j$, and $\mu_{\rm hy}=\alpha\mu_{\rm multi}+(1-\alpha)\mu_{\rm mono}$. For positive standard deviations define
$$G_{\rm multi}=\frac1N\sum_j\frac{R_j-\mu_{\rm multi}}{\sigma_{\rm multi}}S_j,\qquad G_{\rm hy}=\frac1N\sum_j\frac{R_j-\mu_{\rm hy}}{\sigma_{\rm hy}}S_j.$$
Substitution gives exactly
$$G_{\rm hy}=\frac{\sigma_{\rm multi}}{\sigma_{\rm hy}}G_{\rm multi}+\frac{(1-\alpha)\Delta_{IG}}{\sigma_{\rm hy}}\overline S.$$

Take equal batch sizes \(N=M=2\), so \(\alpha=1/2\), with multi-source rewards $(1,2)$ and mono-source rewards $(1,1)$. A Bernoulli policy of success probability $1/4$ with reward $R=1+O$ gives multi-source logit scores $(-1/4,3/4)$; the batch has positive probability. Population standard deviations give
$$\mu_{\rm multi}=\frac32,\quad\mu_{\rm hy}=\frac54,\quad\sigma_{\rm multi}=\frac12,\quad\sigma_{\rm hy}=\frac{\sqrt3}{4},\quad\overline S=\frac14.$$
The actual hybrid update is $5/(4\sqrt3)\approx0.72169$. The standard normalized update is $1/2$, so the printed right-hand side is $1/2+1/16=9/16=0.5625$. The corrected identity gives $5/(4\sqrt3)$ exactly. Neither denominator is zero. With sample standard deviations, as in the inspected implementation, the unstabilized hybrid update is $5/8$, while the printed right-hand side is $1/(2\sqrt2)+1/16$. The discrepancy therefore does not depend on choosing the population convention; a $10^{-6}$ stabilizer cannot bridge these unequal values.
checks.repair:
Retain the divisors actually used by the estimators:
$$G_{\rm hy}=\frac{d_{\rm multi}}{d_{\rm hy}}G_{\rm multi}+\frac{(1-\alpha)\Delta_{IG}}{d_{\rm hy}}\overline S.$$
For positive $d_{\rm multi},d_{\rm hy}$, this follows by adding and subtracting $\mu_{\rm multi}$ in every hybrid numerator. It covers either standard-deviation convention and stabilizers $d=\sigma+\varepsilon$.

Alternatively, state the valid unnormalized identity already derived in Appendix A.3:
$$H_{\rm hy}=H_{\rm multi}+(1-\alpha)\Delta_{IG}\overline S,\qquad H=\frac1N\sum_j(R_j-\mu)S_j.$$
Across batches, random ratios and products must remain inside the expectation. Neither algebraic identity alone proves that the normalized update is the gradient of a fixed information-gain-regularized objective; that interpretation requires a separate argument.
checks.scope: The missing factors invalidate the exact decomposition for the normalized estimator. Appendix A.3's unnormalized identity is correct and is credited here. Restoring scales repairs this algebra, without repairing the separate unbiasedness claim or establishing the stated optimization interpretation.

checks.whyItMatters: The omitted scales change the relative sizes of the two update components. A numerator identity cannot directly justify the normalized decomposition.

checks.claim: Positive rollout updates occur exactly when the multi-source rollout exceeds mono-source performance.
checks.explanation: The mono-source mean shifts the threshold but is not itself the threshold. If the multi-source group performs worse on average, the hybrid mean lies below the mono-source mean. An individual rollout can then receive positive advantage without beating mono-source performance.
checks.demonstration:
Use the paper's counts $N=12$, $M=2$ and its accuracy-plus-format rewards. Let one multi-source rollout receive reward two and the other eleven receive reward one; let both mono-source rollouts receive reward two. Then
$$\mu_{\rm multi}=\frac{13}{12},\quad\mu_{\rm mono}=2,\quad\alpha=\frac67,\quad\mu_{\rm hy}=\frac{17}{14}.$$
The reward-two rollout only matches mono-source performance, yet its centered reward is
$$R_j-\mu_{\rm hy}=\frac{11}{14}>0.$$
With population standard deviation $\sqrt{33}/14$, its advantage is $11/\sqrt{33}>0$. A sample-standard-deviation convention or a positive denominator stabilizer preserves this sign. The individual if-and-only-if claim therefore fails under the stated rollout rule.
checks.repair:
State the individual rule as $A_j^{\rm hy}>0$ if and only if $R_j>\mu_{\rm hy}$, for a positive denominator, where $\mu_{\rm hy}=\alpha\mu_{\rm multi}+(1-\alpha)\mu_{\rm mono}$. A valid group-level comparison is
$$\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N A_j^{\rm hy}=\frac{(1-\alpha)(\mu_{\rm multi}-\mu_{\rm mono})}{d_{\rm hy}}.$$
This follows by averaging the centered rewards and substituting the hybrid mean. For $0\leq\alpha<1$ and $d_{\rm hy}>0$, the mean multi-source advantage has the sign of the mean reward gap, even though individual signs need not. The existing algorithm already implements this rule; the interpretation should distinguish the group mean from individual rollouts.

checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. Verified the algebra of the core derivations and recomputed every reported table average with python3. (i) Entropic OT dual (Eq. 7/14) and optimal primal form Eq. 8 are the standard Sinkhorn dual/plan; substituting the optimum gives Lemma 1 with the 'minus epsilon' term exactly because the optimal plan has total mass 1. (ii) Proposition 2 is a correct application of the envelope/Danskin theorem (only the student marginal term depends explicitly on theta; the additive dual-potential ambiguity cancels because sum_i grad q_i = 0). (iii) Theorem 3 factor check: grad D(p,q) = phi*(p,q).grad q, and the self-term contributes (1/2)*grad D(q,q) = (1/2)*2 phi*(q,q).grad q, so the combined coefficient is phi*(p,q) - phi*(q,q) exactly as Eq. 26/11; the symmetric-cost choice phi*=psi* in the self-transport problem is valid (the problem is invariant under transposing P, and the dual opt set is convex). (iv) I checked that the paper's Dtilde (entropy H(P)=-sum P(log P -1)) and the standard entropically-regularised OT give the same Sinkhorn divergence after self-correction: the extra -epsilon constant and the q,p log-terms cancel exactly in Eq. 6. (v) Table 2 and all three blocks of Table 3 average correctly (e.g. KL row 85.86/5=17.172 -> 17.17; WASD Table 2 112.36/5=22.472 -> 22.47; GPT-2 XL->Base WASD 120.12/5=24.024 -> 24.02). Near-misses deliberately not reported: the claim 'under suitable conditions on the transport cost the Sinkhorn divergence is nonnegative and 0 iff p=q' is hedged and the required conditions on a cosine cost matrix are not stated, but I could not demonstrate the statement false; the reported 23.46 (AMiD) and 29.30 (AMiD, OpenLLaMA2) differ from the means of the displayed rounded cells (23.454, 29.294), which is ordinary rounding of unrounded values, not an error.

checks.contextAfter:
To sum up, the full OptiFlow (Algorithm 1) extracts an effective one-step policy that preserves the multimodal structure of high-value behaviors. It leverages a learned critic (Step 1) and a reference multi-step flow policy (Step 2) to solve per-state optimal transport problems (Step 3). By decoupling value guidance (target marginals) from behavioral geometry (cost matrix), the final transport-guided distillation (Step 4) explicitly maps noise to distinct, in-distribution high-value action modes.
Notably, OptiFlow avoids direct critic maximization, which often exploits unreliable out-of-distribution regions. Instead, it anchors the policy to high-return in-distribution targets via transport plan. This structural separation mitigates the need for explicit behavior regularization while ensuring stable and mode-preserving one-step policy extraction.

checks.claim: The stated W(q) bounds the propagation of local layer-q compression error for every network satisfying Theorem7 assumptions.

The preceding affine-radius recurrence ends at q−1 for the input to layer q. Even a scalar contraction \(x\mapsto\epsilon x\), with zero bias, has output radius \(\epsilon\) times its input radius; no fixed uniform factor permits replacing the latter by the former as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). The needed input-radius factor is therefore not supplied by the printed recurrence.

It is obtained by applying the existing radius bound to layer q−1, followed by the same Lipschitz propagation and telescoping inequalities.

checks.location: Section5 Broader Discussion, Fenchel conjugacy paragraph, text lines506–508
checks.claim: The explicitly defined supremum Fenchel conjugate is concave and its hypograph gives the upper Newton hull.
checks.explanation: The standard supremum conjugate is convex. The concave upper-hull function is \(-p^*\); the sign is missing in the hypograph expression.
checks.demonstration: For \(p(x)=\max(0,x,2x-2)\), the conjugate values at slopes \(0,1,2\) are \(0,0,2\). Concavity would require \(p^*(1)\geq[p^*(0)+p^*(2)]/2=1\), but its value is zero. Moreover, a supporting line with slope a and intercept b obeys \(b\leq-p^*(a)\), so its largest admissible intercept is the negative conjugate.
checks.repair: Call \(p^*\) convex and replace the upper-hypograph expression by \(\operatorname{upper}(\operatorname{hypo}(-p^*))\), over the finite conjugate domain. Then the upper boundary is exactly \(b=-p^*(a)\), matching the correct identity already printed. Use the standard biconjugation formula for reconstruction.
checks.scope: A local sign/convention correction in the discussion, graded Minor. It does not refute the earlier Hausdorff approximation theorem.
